paragraphs.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type V (MEN5) is a syndrome of endocrine and nonendocrine tumors caused by germline pathogenic variants or genomic rearrangements of the MAX gene (Haider et al., 2025). The main feature is pheochromocytoma, which is often bilateral and sometimes metastatic, with or without paraganglioma. Other reported tumors include pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (mainly growth hormone- and/or prolactin-secreting), ganglioneuromas and neuroblastomas, possibly parathyroid adenomas, and nonendocrine tumors (Seabrook et al., 2021; Lian et al., 2024; Charoenngam et al., 2026).

paragraphs.text: Cardot Bauters et al. (2020) reported follow-up of a 3-generation family. The proband developed neuroblastoma of the broad ligament at 17 months of age. At 22 years she developed a right pheochromocytoma, a ganglioneuroma at the site of the original neuroblastoma, and an ileal schwannoma, together with hypertension and high normetanephrine levels. Six years later she had surgery for a left pheochromocytoma associated with a mature ganglioneuroma. She also had a leiomyosarcoma of the mesosigmoid with later cutaneous and other metastases, a hepatic carcinoma at 42 years, and a uterine leiomyoma at 43 years. Her paternal grandfather had bilateral pheochromocytoma at 70 years. Her father had lung adenocarcinoma at 47 years and prostatic cancer at 54 years but never showed an adrenal lesion. Her youngest brother presented at 31 years with a cardiomyopathy complicated by Takotsubo syndrome, which led to the diagnosis of bilateral pheochromocytoma. At 56 years, a paternal uncle was found to have a clinically silent 11-mm hypervascular right adrenal nodule with strong [18F]-DOPA uptake, suggestive of pheochromocytoma or an adrenomedullary nodule.

paragraphs.text: Seabrook et al. (2021) reported 2 families with germline MAX variants evaluated at university hospitals in Australia. In family A, several individuals had pheochromocytoma, including bilateral and metastatic disease. Two children who had not developed pheochromocytoma had neuroendocrine tumors: one had a paravertebral ganglioneuroma and the other an abdominal neuroblastoma. One individual had acromegaly, and his pheochromocytoma tissue stained positive for growth hormone-releasing hormone. Another individual, who had previously had pheochromocytomas resected, had an enlarged pituitary and elevated IGF1. In family B, the proband had bilateral and metastatic pheochromocytoma, a prolactin-producing pituitary tumor, multigland parathyroid adenomas, chondrosarcoma, and multifocal pulmonary adenocarcinomas.

paragraphs.text: Lian et al. (2024) also reviewed 109 patients from 87 families with germline MAX mutations, including their own. Pheochromocytoma developed in 101 patients (92.7%), with a mean age at diagnosis of 32.8 +/- 12.6 years (range, 13-80) and a male-to-female ratio of 1.3:1. Of these, 59 (58.4%) had bilateral tumors: 47 synchronous and 12 metachronous, with a mean interval of 11.1 +/- 6.7 years in the metachronous group. Nineteen (18.8%) had metastatic pheochromocytoma. Eleven patients (10.9%) also had chest or abdominal paraganglioma, and 1 had a head and neck paraganglioma without pheochromocytoma. Nine patients (8.3%) had pituitary neuroendocrine tumors: 3 had elevated growth hormone alone, 4 had elevated prolactin alone, and 1 had both. Eleven patients had other neuroendocrine tumors, diagnosed between 0.7 and 60 years of age. These included primary hyperparathyroidism in 4 patients, and neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma/ganglioneuroma, C-cell hyperplasia, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. Seven patients (6.4%) had non-neuroendocrine tumors, including squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue, papillary thyroid carcinoma, prostate cancer, renal cell carcinoma, renal oncocytoma, and chondrosarcoma with lung adenocarcinoma. Three mutation carriers had no clinical phenotype.
